title: An exchange booth at every step
allegory: A backward function is like an exchange booth at each step of a road: blame for the result arrives in the output's currency, and the booth converts it at its own local rate into blame for each of its inputs.
map: an exchange booth at each step of the road
a backward function registered for each operation
blame arriving in the output's currency
grad_out: the gradient of the loss with respect to this op's output
the booth's exchange rate, set by what passed through it
the local derivative, e.g. 1/x for log, computed from saved forward values
a separate rate for each supplier
one backward function per argument position (for x·y: rate y for x, rate x for y)
converted blame handed to each supplier
the gradient with respect to each input, passed further back
credit: The 'local derivative times the gradient arriving from above' framing follows Andrej Karpathy's micrograd lecture, where each operation stores its own _backward.

chapters.name: Who gets the blame?
chapters.note: nudge every knob and rerun? a million reruns

cap.1: The model's answer is bad. A million knobs made it. Which ones are to blame, and by how much? Nudging each knob and rerunning would take forever.
cap.2: Finite differences needs one forward pass per parameter: fine as a check, hopeless for training. Backprop gets every gradient from a single backward sweep.
cap.3: Finite differences costs O(#params) forward passes. Reverse-mode AD gets the whole gradient of a scalar loss for a small constant multiple of one forward pass, by composing local derivatives.

cap.1: Instead, every operation keeps an exchange booth. Blame arrives from downstream, gets converted at the booth's own rate, and is handed back to its inputs.
cap.2: A backward function takes grad_out (how much the loss cares about this op's output) and returns how much it cares about each input. Each op only needs its own local rate.
cap.3: Each forward op registers a backward mapping grad_out to a gradient per argument: a vector-Jacobian product. No op needs global knowledge; the chain rule is assembled from local pieces.

cap.1: Blame for my input = blame for my output × how fast my output moves when my input moves. That speed is the exchange rate.
cap.2: In code: grad_in = grad_out * local_derivative. For log the local derivative is 1/x, so log_back returns grad_out / x.
cap.3: ∂L/∂x = (∂L/∂out)(∂out/∂x). For tensors this is a vector-Jacobian product, computed without materialising the Jacobian (elementwise ops have a diagonal one).

cap.1: Each kind of booth has its own rule. Multiply has two suppliers, so two rules. Add simply passes the blame straight through to both.
cap.2: exp's rate is its own output, one reason backward functions are handed out too. Two-input ops register one backward per argument position.
cap.3: ARENA dispatches (forward_fn, arg_position) to a backward via a lookup table; signatures take (grad_out, out, *args) so a rate can use saved inputs or the output.

cap.1: Here is log, the booth in your exercise. Near zero it is a cliff: its rate shoots up, so a little blame arriving becomes a flood leaving.
cap.2: log_back is one line, grad_out / x, but that 1/x explodes as x approaches 0. Remember it whenever you take the log of a tiny probability.
cap.3: The 1/x factor is why cross-entropy is computed from logits via log-softmax: fusing the ops keeps forward and backward numerically stable instead of dividing by a tiny p.

chapters.name: Copies send blame home

right.title: Handed back as is
lines: the copies' blame is never added

chapters.verdict: A value used four times gets blame from all four. Sum it home.

cap.1: If the forward pass copied a value four times, all four copies send blame back. The booth must add them up before handing blame to the original.
cap.2: When the forward pass broadcast an input, its gradient comes back in the bigger shape. The backward must unbroadcast: sum over the stretched axes to match the input.
cap.3: Broadcasting is fan-out, so its adjoint is a sum: reduce over the expanded dims (keeping them) and over the prepended ones. Skip it and the gradient comes back the wrong shape for its input.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: loss.backward() runs these booths for you
Fused ops exist to tame steep rates

cap.1: You will rarely write one again: PyTorch has a booth for every operation. But knowing what they do tells you why training breaks when it does.
cap.2: Every loss.backward() runs these conversions in reverse order. Gradients with respect to activations, not just weights, are also how attribution methods ask which parts of a model mattered.
cap.3: Autograd is a library call for life, but reading gradients with respect to activations is a core interpretability tool for understanding, and then steering, what a model relies on.

curves.label: tangent at x: its slope is the booth's rate

caption.1: Slide x and watch the booth's rate, the slope of the orange line. Near zero, log is a cliff: a little blame arriving becomes a lot passed back.
caption.2: log_back returns grad_out / x. The last readout nudges x a tiny bit each way and measures the change directly. They match, and that is how you test any backward function.
caption.3: ∂L/∂x = g/x. The central difference (f(x+h) − f(x−h))/2h agrees to O(h²) and shares no code with your backward, which makes it the reference check. Watch the 1/x blow-up near 0.

where_else: loss.backward() in every training loop: PyTorch runs one of these per operation, in reverse order
Attribution methods in interpretability, which read gradients with respect to activations
Any chain of conversions where rates multiply: currencies, gear trains, unit conversions

hamming.what: A small rule stored with each operation that turns the loss's sensitivity to its output into sensitivity to each of its inputs.
hamming.when: Every time you call loss.backward(), and whenever you write a custom operation or debug a gradient that is too big, too small or the wrong shape.
hamming.why: It turns one global question, which knobs matter, into many tiny local ones that each operation can answer on its own.

object.title: The booth chain
object.subtitle: Two exchange booths on a table, with blame pulsing back from the loss to every input.

nodes.label: × booth: rate w for a, rate a for w
log booth: a = log x, rate 1/x = 2

cap.1: A loss built from two booths: take the log, then multiply by w. Blame starts at the loss as 1 and flows backwards.
cap.2: L = w · log x with x = 0.5 and w = 3. The backward pass starts from dL/dL = 1 and visits each booth in reverse.
cap.3: Reverse mode seeds ∂L/∂L = 1 and applies each op's backward function in reverse topological order.

cap.1: The multiply booth has two suppliers, so two rates: blame for a is multiplied by w, blame for w by a.
cap.2: Multiply's backward is two functions, one per argument: the gradient for a is 1 × w = 3, for w it is 1 × a ≈ −0.69.
cap.3: Backward functions are keyed by (op, argument position); for a·w they are g·w and g·a, each unbroadcast to its input's shape.

cap.1: The log booth's rate is 1/x. At x = 0.5 that is 2, so 3 units of blame arriving become 6 leaving.
cap.2: log_back(grad_out, out, x) returns grad_out / x: here 3 / 0.5 = 6. It needs x, which is why the forward pass keeps its inputs.
cap.3: log_back needs the saved input x, while exp_back can reuse out. Saved tensors are why autograd memory grows with the activations kept.

cap.1: No booth knows the whole road, only its own rate. Chain them and the rates multiply: 1 × 3 × 2 = 6.
cap.2: The chain rule is exactly this: multiply local rates along the path from the loss to an input.
cap.3: ∂L/∂x is the product of local derivatives along the path; with fan-out you sum over paths. That is all reverse-mode autodiff does.

predict.q: x = 0.01 enters the log booth and 1 unit of blame arrives. How much blame leaves for x?
predict.why: log_back returns grad_out / x. Near zero log is steep, so blame is magnified: one reason losses are computed from logits rather than from the log of a tiny probability.

predict.q: Why are backward functions handed the forward output as well as the inputs?

options.t: Some rates are easiest from the output: exp's rate is the output itself
To double-check the forward pass was right

predict.why: The derivative of eˣ is eˣ, which is exactly out, so passing it saves recomputing.
